blocks.text: Stop treating the market like a casino. Start treating it like a partnership deed.
LEVEL 01: NOOB
Forget the BSE screen for a second. Let's talk about Raju's Momo Stall.
Raju makes the best momos in Delhi. He sells 100 plates a day. He wants to open a big shop with AC, but he needs ₹10 Lakhs. He only has ₹5 Lakhs.

You give Raju ₹1 Lakh.
In this simplified example, the share represents 10% of the company’s current shares. Your percentage can change if the company issues more shares or restructures its capital.
That piece of paper is a STOCK.
blocks.title: 🤝 The Deal

blocks.text: If the business earns a profit, it may retain that money or declare a dividend; shareholders do not automatically receive a share of each year’s profit. If the business is sold, the value received by shareholders depends on the sale terms, liabilities, and ownership at that time.

Suppose a company has 1,000 shares and you own 10. You own 1% of the company. Your return depends on what the company does and what buyers later pay for that ownership; the share price is not a guaranteed claim on a fixed amount of cash.

Critical Truth: The Secondary Market
When you buy a share of Tata Motors on Zerodha/Upstox, Tata Motors does NOT get your money.

You are buying it from another person (Uncle Sharma) who wants to sell it. In the secondary market, investors trade existing shares with one another. A company can also raise capital later through offers such as a follow-on issue, rights issue, or other permitted issuance.

When a company issues new shares, it can raise capital. When investors trade existing shares with one another, ownership changes hands. Before investing, ask which event is happening and whether new shares may dilute existing ownership.
blocks.title: 🧾 Primary vs Secondary

blocks.text: LEVEL 03: PRO
How do you know if a stock is cheap or expensive? You use the P/E Ratio.

Imagine a Shirt generates ₹10 of rent per year (Earnings).
- Case A: At ₹200 per share and ₹10 earnings per share, P/E is 20.
- Case B: At ₹1,000 per share and the same ₹10 earnings per share, P/E is 100. The multiple is higher; whether that price is justified depends on growth, risk, and other evidence.
P/E = Price you pay for ₹1 of Earning.
blocks.title: 👕 The Shirt Analogy

blocks.text: Market Cap (Size Matters)
Small Cap: Like a Speedboat. Fast, can turn easily, but flips over in a storm.
Large Cap: Like an Oil Tanker (Titanic). Slow, stable, survives storms, but takes 5km to turn.

Compare companies with similar business models, growth prospects, and risks. A lower P/E can reflect slower growth or higher uncertainty; a higher P/E can reflect optimism. The ratio is a starting question, not a buy or sell signal.
blocks.title: 🧠 Valuation Check

blocks.text:
This is what banks don't teach you.
1. The Free Float Trap
A company may have a large market capitalisation but a small free float if insiders hold most shares. A smaller free float can mean less trading liquidity and more price sensitivity to orders; it does not by itself prove price manipulation.
2. ASM/GSM Lists (The Jail)
Exchanges apply surveillance measures using multiple, changing criteria. Inclusion is a market-surveillance action, not a finding of wrongdoing. Applicable trading restrictions depend on the current exchange framework; check the latest NSE ASM information before trading.
blocks.title: ☠️ GOD MODE: The 1% Knowledge

blocks.text: Write down the business you think you are buying, why its earnings could grow, what could prove your view wrong, and how much loss you could tolerate. Revisit the reasons when the business changes, not only when the price moves.
